text: If superposition alone gave you computational power, every quantum algorithm would be a free exponential speedup for everything, all the time. That isn't true, and understanding exactly why separates a real grasp of quantum computing from the myth.

The claim you'll hear constantly: put n qubits into superposition and the computer tries all 2 to the n answers in parallel, then just reads off the right one. The first part is real — a uniform superposition really does have nonzero amplitude on every basis state at once. But you can't simply read off the correct one. Measuring collapses the system to one random string sampled by the Born rule, and if all the amplitudes are equal, that's a uniformly random guess, no better than flipping coins. Superposition by itself buys you nothing at readout time.

The real engine is interference: amplitudes are complex numbers that add up, and can reinforce or cancel before you ever measure. A well-designed algorithm applies a specific sequence of gates engineered so the correct answer's amplitude grows across multiple steps while wrong answers get driven toward cancellation. Only after that amplification and cancellation does the algorithm measure, when the probability of getting the right answer is overwhelmingly large.

That's why speedups are specific, not automatic. Shor's algorithm exploits periodicity using the quantum Fourier transform, giving an exponential speedup for factoring specifically. Grover's algorithm gives a quadratic speedup, roughly root N queries instead of N, for unstructured search, and it's provably the best any quantum algorithm can do for that problem. Neither is just classical-plus-superposition — each exploits a specific mathematical structure, and more qubits running the wrong algorithm buys you nothing.

Next lesson puts classical and quantum information side by side with exact numbers at the same system size, three bits versus three qubits, so you can see precisely where they match and where they diverge.
